incidents.title: Budget gone, pager silent
incidents.brief: Checkout errors jump to 2% while CPU sits at 41%. No page fires because every alert watches CPU. At this rate the 99.9% SLO's 43-minute monthly budget is gone in 36 hours.
incidents.constraint: Page for user pain, not busy machines; payment-provider blips burn up to 8x for an hour and heal.
incidents.question: What should page the on-call engineer?

choices.label: Page on error-budget burn rate in 1 h and 5 min windows
choices.resultTitle: Paged within the hour, not in 36
choices.resultBody: A 2% error rate burns the 0.1% budget at 20x. With a 14x threshold the 1 h window crosses it about 42 minutes in, the 5 min window confirms the burn is still happening, and the alert clears once errors stop.

choices.label: Lower the CPU alert threshold from 80% to 35% on checkout
choices.resultTitle: Paged all day for nothing
choices.resultBody: Checkout runs at 41% CPU on every normal afternoon, so the pager fires daily while a real error spike at 30% CPU stays silent.

choices.label: Page when checkout errors exceed 1,000 per minute
choices.resultTitle: Quiet at night, loud at noon
choices.resultBody: At 18,000 req/s the 2% spike is 21,600 errors a minute and pages, but at 3 a.m. traffic the same 2% never crosses 1,000.

hints: Is 41% CPU a problem for a shopper?
The SLO says how many failures a month you can afford.
Alert on how fast that allowance is being spent, over a long and a short window.

knob.label: 1 h burn-rate page threshold
knob.question: Pick the 1 h burn threshold: ignore 8x provider blips, page on this 20x burn within 50 minutes.

low.title: Paged for blips that heal themselves
low.body: Below 10x, payment-provider wobbles that burn up to 8x for an hour cross the threshold, so on-call is woken several times a week for errors that clear on their own, and soon starts ignoring the pager.

high.title: The 20x burn pages too late, or never
high.body: At a 20x burn the 1 h window reaches a threshold T after 3 x T minutes. Above 16x that is more than 50 minutes, and at 20x or higher this outage never pages while the 36-hour budget drains.

good.title: Paged in 30 to 48 minutes, blips ignored
good.body: At a 20x burn the 1 h window crosses T after 3 x T minutes, so a 10-16x threshold pages within 30-48 minutes, having spent only 1.4-2.2% of the month's budget, while 8x provider blips never fire.

incidents.title: The p99 that averaged away
incidents.brief: The dashboard shows search p99 at 180 ms by averaging p99 across 40 hosts. Users report 1.4 s searches. Three hosts with a bad disk serve 8% of traffic.
incidents.constraint: The fleet p99 must reflect what the slowest 1% of requests actually felt.
incidents.question: How should the fleet-wide p99 be computed?

choices.label: Merge per-host latency histograms, then read p99
choices.resultTitle: The real tail shows up
choices.resultBody: Merged histograms put the fleet p99 at 1.4 s, matching user reports and pointing straight at the three bad-disk hosts.

choices.label: Report the slowest host's p99 as the fleet-wide p99
choices.resultTitle: One host sets the number
choices.resultBody: The worst host alone reads 2.1 s even though it serves under 3% of requests, so the chart overstates the tail and jumps with every noisy box.

nodes.sub: its 2.1 s is now the fleet p99

choices.label: Average the host p99s weighted by each host's request count
choices.resultTitle: Still an average of tails
choices.resultBody: Weighting nudges the number to 290 ms, but percentiles do not average: 8% of requests at 1.4 s still hides under a value users never see.

hints: Is an average of 40 percentiles itself a percentile?
You need the raw distribution, not 40 summaries of it.
Combine bucket counts from every host before picking the 99th percentile.

variants.constraint: Tracing storage costs exceed $15,000/month because 99.9% of traces represent fast, uninteresting 200 OK requests.

obs-02-tail-sample.resultTitle: Tail-based sampling keeps errors and slow spans while cutting 90% of cost
obs-02-tail-sample.resultBody: Sampling traces at the tail buffers traces in memory and saves only errors or p99 outliers, slashing storage bills.

obs-02-sample-all.resultTitle: 100% trace sampling exhausted logging storage budgets
obs-02-sample-all.resultBody: Ingesting billions of healthy 200 OK traces created massive network egress and disk retention costs with minimal diagnostic value.

incidents.title: Fourteen services, no culprit
incidents.brief: Checkout p99 rose from 400 ms to 2.8 s after a deploy. The request crosses 14 services and each team's dashboard looks green. Nobody can see where the 2.4 s goes.
incidents.constraint: Find the slow hop without redeploying all 14 services twice.
incidents.question: What gives the team the per-hop breakdown?

choices.label: Propagate a trace id header and record spans per hop
choices.resultTitle: Tax service caught waiting
choices.resultBody: The trace waterfall shows 2.3 s inside the tax service waiting on a new lock; rolling it back brings p99 from 2.8 s to 420 ms.

choices.label: Add latency dashboards for each of the 14 services
choices.resultTitle: Fourteen green dashboards
choices.resultBody: Each service's own average looks fine because the slow calls are a small share of its traffic, so nothing links the 2.8 s requests together.

choices.label: Turn on debug-level request logging in all 14 services
choices.resultTitle: Logs pile up, still unlinked
choices.resultBody: Log volume grows 9x and CPU climbs to 52%, but with no shared id nobody can stitch one slow checkout's lines together across services.

hints: Each service is healthy on average. Which request is slow?
You need to follow one request across every hop.
Pass one id through every call and time each span.

incidents.title: The errors tracing never saw
incidents.brief: 0.05% of payments time out after 6 s. Tracing keeps a random 1% chosen at the gateway, so 99% of the 170k daily failures have no trace, including every one support asks about.
incidents.constraint: Tracing storage may grow at most 20%.
incidents.question: How should traces be sampled?

choices.label: Tail-sample all errors and slow traces, 1% of the rest
choices.resultTitle: Every failure has a trace
choices.resultBody: Deciding after the request finishes keeps all 170,000 failed payments a day plus a 1% baseline, so storage grows about 5% instead of 100x.

choices.label: Raise head sampling at the gateway from 1% to 100%
choices.resultTitle: Storage bill up 100x
choices.resultBody: Every one of 345 million daily requests is stored, the span pipeline backs up and the trace store costs a hundred times the 20% budget.

choices.label: Head-sample 1% of users by hashing the user id
choices.resultTitle: Still guessing up front
choices.resultBody: Hashing makes traces consistent per user, but the choice is still made before anyone knows the request will fail, so 99% of failures vanish.

hints: When does the gateway decide to keep a trace?
At that moment, does it know the request will fail?
Decide after the request completes, based on its outcome.

incidents.title: A label that ate the TSDB
incidents.brief: A team added user_id as a label on http_requests_total. 2 M users x 30 endpoints x 5 status codes is 300 M series. The metrics store OOMs and the bill is up 12x.
incidents.constraint: Keep per-user debugging possible without per-user metric series.
incidents.question: What is the right fix?

choices.label: Drop user_id from metrics; put it on traces and logs
choices.resultTitle: Back to 3,000 series
choices.resultBody: Without user_id the counter has 150 series per host, store memory falls from 93% to 40%, and per-user questions go to trace and log search.

choices.label: Triple the metrics store's memory and shard it three ways
choices.resultTitle: Store stable at 80%, series still climbing
choices.resultBody: Tripled memory and three shards bring the store to 80% and the OOMs stop tonight. Series still grow with every signup, about 4% a week, and the metrics bill is now 36x what it was last month.

choices.label: Keep user_id but scrape every 5 minutes instead of 15 s
choices.resultTitle: Same series, blurrier data
choices.resultBody: Cost comes from the 300 M distinct series, not the scrape rate, so memory stays at 90% while alerts now lag by five minutes.

hints: What multiplies to make 300 M?
Every unique label combination is its own series.
Keep unbounded ids out of metric labels; they belong on events.

culprit.explanation: The API fleet's 14:05 deploy added user_id to http_requests_total, and its /metrics output jumped from 180 KB to 41 MB per scrape. The store is only drowning in the series that one label creates.

wrongNodeFeedback.tsdb: The store is the victim: it is OOMing on the series it was handed. Find what started creating them at 14:05.
wrongNodeFeedback.q: The pipeline is backed up because the samples behind it exploded. Look upstream.
wrongNodeFeedback.dash: On-call only sees the fallout: slow dashboards and late alerts.

tsdb: OOMKilled: memory limit reached, replaying WAL
dash: dashboard queries timing out after 60 s

incidents.title: Forty minutes to find one order
incidents.brief: Support escalates 'order 88213 failed'. Free-text logs from 60 pods add up to 9 TB a day, and grepping for the order number takes 40 minutes and misses lines that never print it.
incidents.constraint: Answer a single-request question in under a minute.
incidents.question: What makes one request's logs findable?

choices.label: Emit JSON logs carrying an indexed request id field
choices.resultTitle: One query, 12 lines
choices.resultBody: Each line now has request_id, order_id and service fields, so a single indexed lookup returns all 12 lines for order 88213 in two seconds.

choices.label: Grep all 60 pods in parallel with a faster regex
choices.resultTitle: Faster search, same gaps
choices.resultBody: Parallel grep cuts the wait to eight minutes and spikes log cluster CPU to 70%, yet lines that never mention 88213 are still missed.

choices.label: Raise log retention from 7 days to 30 days
choices.resultTitle: More haystack, no needle
choices.resultBody: Keeping 9 TB a day for 30 days quadruples storage and makes each grep slower, while nothing ties one request's lines together.

hints: Which lines of this order never print the order number?
Something must follow the request into every log line.
Give every line machine-readable fields, including one shared id.

incidents.title: Prometheus crash-loops and alerts go blind
incidents.brief: Opsline onboarded three services; Prometheus active series rose from 1.2M to 2.6M, all with bounded labels. The 16 GB server now OOMs every 2 h and each WAL replay blinds alerts for 12 minutes.
incidents.constraint: The new series are legitimate and needed; alerting cannot stay blind tonight.
incidents.question: What gets alerting reliable again tonight?

choices.label: Upsize Prometheus to a 64 GB memory-optimized instance tonight
choices.resultTitle: Head block fits, crash loop ends
choices.resultBody: 2.6M series need roughly 10 GB of head memory plus headroom for queries, compaction and WAL replay, which a 16 GB box cannot give. On 64 GB memory peaks at 35% and no evaluations are missed. Cost: about $450 a month more, revisited when series pass 8M.

choices.label: Shard Prometheus by service with Thanos querying across shards
choices.resultTitle: A two-week project started at midnight
choices.resultBody: Sharding needs new scrape configs, object storage, sidecars and rewritten cross-service alert rules. None of it is ready tonight, so the single server keeps crash-looping and alerts stay blind 12 minutes out of every 2 hours.

choices.label: Drop the pod label and keep only per-service recording rules
choices.resultTitle: Memory fits, per-pod alerts vanish
choices.resultBody: Series fall to 0.9M and the OOMs stop, but the three new services' per-pod saturation and crash-loop alerts depended on that label. Two of them now cannot fire, so a single bad pod hides inside a healthy service average.

hints: The series count grew for a good reason and will not shrink.
Prometheus keeps every active series in memory in its head block.
Compare the memory that 2.6M series need with what the server has.

incidents.title: Paged at 3 a.m. for two failed requests
incidents.brief: Burn-rate paging now covers every service. The internal refunds API gets 40 requests an hour at night; 2 failures read as a 50x burn and page on-call three nights running.
incidents.constraint: Refunds keeps its 99.9% SLO, and a real refunds outage must still page.
incidents.question: How do you keep burn-rate paging honest on tiny traffic?

choices.label: Require a minimum failure count before a burn alert pages

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A rate needs enough events to mean anything; a count floor keeps tiny services quiet.

choices.resultTitle: Stray errors open tickets, outages still page
choices.resultBody: The alert now also needs at least 10 failed requests in the hour, so 2 stray errors out of 40 open a ticket instead of waking anyone. A real outage fails every request and still pages within the hour. Cost: small partial failures on tiny services are caught more slowly.

choices.label: Raise every service's page threshold from a 14x to a 60x burn
choices.resultTitle: Checkout's real burn goes silent too
choices.resultBody: Refunds stops paging, but checkout's 20x burn can never cross 60x either, so its budget drains without a page: the same blind spot you started the week with.

choices.label: Mute the refunds API's burn alerts from midnight to 6 a.m.
choices.resultTitle: A real night outage goes unseen
choices.resultBody: Nights go quiet until a certificate expires at 02:10 on Friday: refunds fail completely, nobody is paged for five hours, and about 200 refunds fail before the day shift notices.

hints: Two failures out of forty is a 5% error rate: a big rate built on tiny numbers.
A real outage on this service fails every request, not two of them.
Pair the burn-rate condition with a floor on how many requests actually failed.

incidents.title: Kept failure traces arrive in pieces
incidents.brief: Tail sampling runs on 6 collectors behind a round-robin balancer. A trace's spans land on different collectors, so each decides alone: 40% of kept failure traces are missing spans, and collectors hit 92% memory.
incidents.constraint: Trace storage may grow at most 20%, and payment timeouts take 6 s.
incidents.question: How do all of a trace's spans reach one sampling decision?

choices.label: Route spans by trace ID so one collector sees each trace

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Consistent routing by trace ID; a sampler restart loses the traces it was buffering.

choices.resultTitle: One trace, one sampler, one decision
choices.resultBody: A load-balancing exporter tier hashes trace_id, so every span of a trace reaches the same sampler, which decides once with the whole trace in view. Partial kept traces fall from 40% to under 1%, and memory drops to 60% because each span is buffered once. Cost: one small extra collector tier.

choices.label: Cut the sampler's decision wait from 30 s to 2 s
choices.resultTitle: Decided before the slow spans exist
choices.resultBody: Memory falls to 50%, but payment timeouts take 6 s, so the sampler decides before the slow spans arrive and throws away exactly the timed-out traces support keeps asking about.

nodes.sub: decides at 2 s, timeouts at 6 s

choices.label: Double each collector's memory and keep round-robin routing
choices.resultTitle: Memory alarm clears, traces still split
choices.resultBody: The memory alarm clears for $500 a month more, but spans of one trace still land on different collectors that decide independently, so 40% of kept failure traces still arrive in pieces.

hints: Each collector can only judge the spans it received.
A round-robin balancer spreads one trace's spans across all six collectors.
Make the routing key the thing the decision is about.

incidents.title: The metrics store OOMs again, on all shards
incidents.brief: Tripling the metrics store bought six weeks. A signup campaign added 1.4M users; user_id series hit 510M, all three shards OOM in turn, and alert rules have been blind for 20 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Support still needs per-user debugging, and there is no budget for more memory this quarter.
incidents.question: What stops metric series from growing with the user count?

choices.label: Hotfix the API to drop user_id; look users up in traces

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded metric labels; per-user questions move to traces and logs.

choices.resultTitle: Series fall back to thousands
choices.resultBody: The hotfix rolls out in 20 minutes and each host goes back to about 150 series for the counter. The 510M old series age out of the head block within two hours, memory settles at 35%, and support finds a user's requests by searching traces and logs by user_id.

choices.label: Set a sample_limit on the API scrape job to cap its series
choices.resultTitle: Every API metric goes dark
choices.resultBody: The API scrape now exceeds its limit every time, and Prometheus rejects the whole scrape: every API metric goes stale, including the error-rate series the burn-rate alerts need. Memory recovers; visibility is gone.

choices.label: Hash user_id into 1,000 buckets so the label stays bounded
choices.resultTitle: Bounded series, useless per-user data
choices.resultBody: Series drop to about 3M and the store recovers, but each bucket mixes some 3,400 users, so the per-user charts support relies on show noise and the real fix still has to ship.

hints: Series count is every label's values multiplied together; one of them grows with signups.
More memory only moves the date of the next OOM.
Keep per-user ids in traces and logs, not in metric labels.

incidents.title: High-cardinality user_id label explodes Prometheus TSDB memory
incidents.brief: A developer adds `user_id` as a label to an HTTP request duration histogram, creating 15 million new time series that crash the Prometheus TSDB.
incidents.constraint: Retain per-user debugging telemetry without exhausting TSDB memory.
incidents.question: How should high-cardinality data be partitioned between metrics and traces?

choices.label: Drop user_id from metric labels and attach it to distributed trace spans
choices.resultTitle: Metrics cardinality collapsed; tracing captured user context
choices.resultBody: Metrics require low-cardinality aggregation (e.g. status code, route); high-cardinality values belong in trace attributes or logs.

choices.label: Shorten Prometheus scrape interval from 15 seconds to 1 second
choices.resultTitle: Faster scrape interval multiplied ingest load by 15x
choices.resultBody: Scraping 15 million time series every 1 second triggered immediate unrecoverable out-of-memory crashes on all scrape workers.

choices.label: Set TSDB storage retention to 5 minutes so time series purge immediately
choices.resultTitle: Short retention destroyed historical observability dashboards
choices.resultBody: Purging data after 5 minutes made alerting rules, trend analysis, and incident post-mortems completely impossible.

hints: TSDB memory scales with the number of unique label combinations (series cardinality).
A label with millions of distinct values (like user_id, order_id, or email) destroys time series databases.
Keep metrics bounded to low-cardinality tags (tier, status_code, region) and place IDs in traces.

incidents.title: Head-based trace sampling discards rare 5xx error traces
incidents.brief: A 1% head-based probabilistic sampling rule discards 99% of requests at ingress, causing SREs to miss rare critical 500 error payment failures.
incidents.constraint: Capture 100% of error and anomalous high-latency spans without inflating trace storage bills.
incidents.question: Which sampling strategy guarantees retention of all error and outlier traces?

choices.label: Deploy tail-based sampling collector to inspect traces upon completion
choices.resultTitle: Tail-based sampling preserved 100% of failed traces
choices.resultBody: Tail sampling buffers completed traces in memory, saving 100% of 5xx errors and slow outliers while sampling healthy 200s at 1%.

choices.label: Set head-based sampling rate to 100% for all incoming requests globally
choices.resultTitle: 100% trace sampling exploded network and backend storage bills
choices.resultBody: Ingesting 35,000 full spans per second generated 15TB of trace data daily, blowing past monthly infrastructure budgets.

choices.label: Disable distributed tracing and rely entirely on stdout console logs
choices.resultTitle: Console logs lost microservice causality and latency breakdowns
choices.resultBody: Without distributed trace IDs, debugging asynchronous multi-hop RPC failures required tedious manual log correlation.

hints: Head-based sampling decides whether to keep a trace at the root before knowing if it will error.
Tail-based sampling collects spans into a buffer and decides based on the final HTTP status code and latency.
Tail sampling ensures 100% visibility into errors with low overall data volume.

incidents.title: Collector agent backpressure drops unbuffered telemetry metrics
incidents.brief: During network blips to the observability SaaS vendor, local OpenTelemetry collector agents run out of memory buffer and drop millions of customer metrics.
incidents.constraint: Buffer telemetry during network blips without exhausting node memory.
incidents.question: How should OpenTelemetry collector queues be configured for resilience?

choices.label: Configure file_storage disk-backed queue extension in collector exporter
choices.resultTitle: Persistent disk queue absorbed network outage cleanly
choices.resultBody: Disk-backed exporter queues spool telemetry to local storage during vendor outages and replay automatically upon reconnection.

choices.label: Configure drop_oldest policy to discard metrics immediately when RAM fills
choices.resultTitle: Silently dropping metrics created blind spots during incidents
choices.resultBody: Discarding data left operators with zero telemetry during the exact network outage periods when monitoring was most needed.

choices.label: Block calling application HTTP worker threads until telemetry delivers
choices.resultTitle: Blocking application threads propagated telemetry outage to users
choices.resultBody: User requests froze waiting for telemetry exports, turning an internal observability blip into a total customer-facing outage.

hints: In-memory queues in telemetry collectors quickly overflow when downstream endpoints slow down.
Disk-backed queues (`file_storage` in OTel) buffer data persistently without increasing JVM/Go heap.
Telemetry export must always remain asynchronous and never block foreground request handlers.

incidents.title: Unindexed debug logs saturate log aggregation cluster ingest
incidents.brief: A release deployed with `DEBUG` logging enabled outputs 250,000 log lines/second, flooding Kafka and elasticsearch log clusters and blowing disk quotas.
incidents.constraint: Filter unnecessary debug chatter without redeploying microservices.
incidents.question: How should dynamic log throttling be applied at the telemetry pipeline layer?

choices.label: Deploy filterprocessor rule in collector pipeline to drop level == debug
choices.resultTitle: Pipeline filter dropped debug flood before cluster ingest
choices.resultBody: Filtering out non-essential debug payloads at the local collector agent reduced ingest volume by 80% without microservice rebuilds.

choices.label: Double log aggregation cluster node count to absorb the debug stream
choices.resultTitle: Doubling cluster size dramatically increased infrastructure costs
choices.resultBody: Paying thousands of dollars to store repetitive debug chatter was economically wasteful and filled disks with noise.

choices.label: Turn off logging agent across all nodes and rely purely on SSH access
choices.resultTitle: Killing logging agent blinded engineers to real production errors
choices.resultBody: Disabling log aggregation prevented operations from seeing fatal errors and audit access records, violating compliance.

hints: Collector pipelines (FluentBit, Logstash, Vector, OTel) allow declarative filtering rules.
Dropping debug logs at the edge stops network transit and backend indexing costs.
Production systems should emit INFO, WARN, and ERROR by default.

incidents.title: Missing W3C traceparent headers cause broken trace spans
incidents.brief: Calls routed through an internal legacy reverse proxy strip unknown headers, breaking distributed trace trees into fragmented single-hop spans.
incidents.constraint: Preserve end-to-end trace correlation across all internal microservice gateways.
incidents.question: How should header propagation be standardized across distributed proxies?

choices.label: Configure proxy to forward W3C traceparent and tracestate headers
choices.resultTitle: W3C headers restored end-to-end trace correlation
choices.resultBody: Forwarding standard `traceparent` headers allows downstream services to attach child spans to the existing parent trace ID seamlessly.

choices.label: Encode trace context into custom session cookies encrypted by backend
choices.resultTitle: Cookie context failed for asynchronous background worker jobs
choices.resultBody: Cookies only work for browser HTTP requests, breaking context propagation for Kafka consumers and gRPC services.

choices.label: Instruct backend services to generate fresh root trace IDs unconditionally
choices.resultTitle: Generating fresh roots made distributed tracing useless
choices.resultBody: Creating independent trace IDs at every hop eliminated the caller-callee relationship, making end-to-end latency inspection impossible.

hints: W3C Trace Context defines `traceparent` (version, trace_id, parent_id, trace_flags).
If an intermediate proxy drops the header, downstream services assume they are the root of a new trace.
Ensure all reverse proxies, load balancers, and API gateways pass trace headers transparently.
